title: Eastern Southampton: English Settlement and Shinnecock Land Rights
summary: English settlers from Lynn and later Southampton trustees claimed Shinnecock land through the 1640 deed and 1703 release. Read those documents alongside disputed boundaries, the thousand-year lease, township-wide gathering rights and the Shinnecock Nation’s continuing homeland.

why_this_matters: The same records that asserted colonial title preserved Native planting and gathering rights. Connecting them to the living Shinnecock Nation changes this landscape from a story of vanished people into one of dispossession, negotiation, continuing landholding and responsibility.

history_title: English claims, contested boundaries and continuing Shinnecock rights
history_content:
A Native homeland beneath familiar Hamptons names

Southampton village, Water Mill, Bridgehampton and the Southampton side of Sag Harbor lie within a landscape whose Native history did not begin with the English town. Shinnecock, Sebonac, Mecox and Niamug appear in the records through which colonists claimed land and Native people continued to assert relationships to it. This chapter follows the eastern mainland from Canoe Place toward the East Hampton town line. Its outline is a reading area, not the boundary of one sale. The Shinnecock Nation continues to govern and care for land at Shinnecock Neck and Westwoods today. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, printed pp. 12–14 Records of the Town of Southampton, Third Book, printed pp. 372–374 Shinnecock Indian Nation

Who established the English settlement?

The newcomers were English colonists arriving from Lynn, Massachusetts, in 1640. Before their agreement with Shinnecock leaders, they sought permission through James Farret, agent for William Alexander, Earl of Stirling, whose claim rested on a grant from Charles I of England. That European chain of authority did not originate with the Native owners. The settlers subsequently secured a separate document with Native leaders. Reading both claims together shows how colonization joined outside assertions of sovereignty to locally negotiated agreements. Historic Documents: Southampton The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, printed pp. 9–11

The December 13, 1640 deed names John Gosmer, Edward Howell, Daniell How, Edward Needham, Thomas Halsey, John Cooper, Thomas Sayre, Edward Farrington, Job Sayre, George Welbee, Allen Breade, William Harker and Henry Walton as the English parties. Its opening names Pomatuck, Mandush, Mocomanto, Pathemanto, Wybbenett, Wainmenowog, Heden, Watemexoted and Checkepuchat as Native parties; spellings vary elsewhere in the records. The document acknowledged sixteen coats already received, promised sixty bushels of corn by September 1641, and committed the English to defend the Native parties against unjust attacks by other Native people. It combined material payments, a political obligation and the English language of permanent, inheritable title. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, printed pp. 12–14

An agreement did not settle every boundary or relationship

The 1640 text begins at the canoe portage between the bays, now associated with Canoe Place, and extends eastward without a precise eastern survey line. A memorandum also preserved Native planting liberty west of a creek on the west side of Shinnecock Plain. Neither the payment nor the document means that all Native relationships to the land ended on that date. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, printed pp. 13–14

Shinnecock food stores and wells were on the plain the settlers had divided. On April 6, 1641, the town ordered anyone holding lots on Shinecock Plain where "any Indian Barnes or welles" lay open to fill them up by April 10, so that cattle would not be hurt. The records' editor, William S. Pelletreau, explains that these barns were holes dug in the earth and lined with bark for keeping corn through the winter, covered with rushes. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, printed p. 22

On June 19, 1657, the town recorded an answer from an unnamed Native man appointed by a sachem and the woman accompanying him: questioned by the English, they placed the earlier bounds at George Cake or Wainscott, or thereabouts. The entry names English witnesses John Howell, Richard Howell, Obadiah Rogers, Joseph Rainer and Samuel Clark, but leaves the Native speakers unnamed. This is evidence of the town's continuing effort to establish the eastern extent of its claim, not a modern surveyed boundary or proof that every Native rights-holder agreed. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, printed pp. 114

Shinnecock Neck, 1663

On March 14, 1663, a Southampton town meeting ordered "that ye Indians shall bee fenced into Shinecock great neck to plant on." The same day the town agreed that no one would settle or keep a farm within its new Quogue purchase from Captain John Scott. Shinnecock Neck is where the Shinnecock Nation's territory is today. The Second Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, printed p. 39

A shared fence beside Shinnecock fields

Shinnecock families kept planting their own fields within the bounds the town claimed. On December 26, 1677, Southampton drew lots to divide the fence it had to build at Shinnecock "against the land which ye Indians plant." Each household was assigned a length by the size of its lot, five poles for a £150 lot, beginning at the creek opposite Thomas Halsey's close and running north and then west "till it meets with ye stake where ye Indians begins." The Second Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, printed p. 264

A complaint the town sent to New York's governor on November 20, 1680 explains the arrangement: under an earlier covenant, wherever the Shinnecock planted within Southampton's bounds, the town was to fence one half and the Shinnecock the other. The town asked the governor to make the Shinnecock plant in one convenient place and fence their half. The Shinnecock were heard before the governor on December 10, 1680, but the printed record does not preserve their answer. Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York, vol. XIV, printed p. 756

In 1703, town trustees sought a broader release

The town's own account says its trustees met Shinnecock representatives on August 13, 1703, over Native dissatisfaction concerning their land. After debate, the meeting adjourned and negotiations continued. The resulting release, dated August 16, describes a broad township claim reaching east to the East Hampton line near Wainscott. Additional acknowledgments and payments followed on August 21. This was a later effort to consolidate colonial title, not simply a repetition of a complete transfer supposedly finished in 1640. Records of the Town of Southampton, Second Book, printed pp. 176–180 Records of the Town of Southampton, Second Book, printed pp. 358–359

Native leaders recorded as Pomquamo, Chice and Mahanum appear in these instruments, with spelling variants in the lease and accounts. The receiving town trustees included Elnathan Topping, Joseph Fordham, Joseph Pierson, Abraham Howell, Jeckamiah Scott, Josiah Howell, Daniel Halsey, Thomas Stephens, Joseph Howell, Gershum Culver, John Malbie and Hezekiah Howell. The release specifies twenty pounds. The separate negotiation account lists additional distributions and expenses, including an interpreter and drink for the Native participants, trustees and witnesses. The records reveal an organized town effort to obtain documentary title; they do not, by themselves, tell us what every participant understood or prove free consent by everyone with an interest in the land. Records of the Town of Southampton, Second Book, printed pp. 176–180 Records of the Town of Southampton, Second Book, printed pp. 358–359

The thousand-year lease reveals what a “sale” leaves out

The companion August 16, 1703 lease covered land called Shinnecock and Sebonnuck, east of Canoe Place between the bays. It named Pomguama, Chice and Manaman and their people as the Native parties. Southampton's trustees framed themselves as landlords, charging one ear of corn each November 1 for a thousand-year term. This changed the legal framing of Native occupation: people with ancestral relationships to the land appeared in the English instrument as tenants of the town. Records of the Town of Southampton, Third Book, printed pp. 372–373

The lease protected planting and timber for fuel and fencing, while excepting such resources as meadows, marshes, pasture, timber, stone and highways from its grant. Native enclosures could not remain fenced between the end of October and April 1. These overlapping, unequal rights were more complicated than either unrestricted private ownership or an empty landscape surrendered to settlers. A further clause protected Shinnecock gathering of reeds and grasses used for mats and houses, and digging groundnuts, throughout the township except mowing land. That township-wide provision matters well beyond the smaller lease area. Records of the Town of Southampton, Third Book, printed pp. 372–373

Continuing land, governance and responsibility

The lease is part of the later story of Shinnecock Hills and its loss, told in the linked Shinnecock Hills article. It is not the whole story of eastern Southampton, and Native landholding did not disappear. The Nation identifies Shinnecock Neck and Westwoods as its continuing territories. In January 2025 it announced federal reaffirmation of Westwoods as restricted-fee land held by the Nation, rather than a newly returned parcel. Shinnecock Indian Nation Land Determination

Follow the Shinnecock Indian Reservation, Shinnecock Hills and Sebonac Creek articles to connect these documents to community life, dispossession and continuing relationships with land and water. Learning this history means distinguishing a colonial claim, a recorded payment, retained resource rights and present-day Native jurisdiction. None is interchangeable with the others. The First Book of Records of the Town of Southampton, printed pp. 12–14 Records of the Town of Southampton, Third Book, printed pp. 372–373 Shinnecock Indian Nation
whereintheworld_content: The shaded area covers today's Southampton mainland east of western Southampton, to the shoreline. It includes Southampton village, Water Mill, Bridgehampton and the Southampton portion of Sag Harbor for regional orientation. It is not a reconstruction of the 1640 deed, the uncertain 1657 eastern limit, or the smaller 1703 lease. Shinnecock Reservation and Westwoods are excluded from this colonial land-history outline and remain separately interpreted Native land. Detached islands are omitted; connected coastal beaches follow the modern shoreline. Historic shorelines and boundaries changed; the shape neither establishes current ownership nor grants access to private or tribal property. NYS Civil Boundaries: Towns and Cities
